mentions.sentence: Indeed, recent years have witnessed a surge of research efforts for testing GDBMSs [18,32,35,36].
mentions.context_before: ate efficient storing and querying graph data that consists of vertices and edges. Hence, recent years have witnessed an ever-growing usage of GDBMSs in various datadriven applications, such as recommendation systems [ 26, 48], fraud detection [ 44], and program analysis [ 59]. As stated by the industry report [ 3], the market of graph database is forecast to reach USD 88.9 billion by 2030. For instance, Neo4j [7], the most popular and widely adopted GDBMSs, has been adopted by over 1,000 enterprise customers. GDBMSs are complex software systems like compilers, and thus are not immune to bugs.
mentions.context_after: and numerous bugs in industrial GDBMSs have been reported. Existing techniques focus on integrating test oracles to identify bugs, and can be divided into two main strands: differential testing (DT) and metamorphic testing (MT). For multiple implementations of a single specification, DT provides the same valid input to these implementations and observes differences in their executions to detect bugs. For multiple implementations of a single specification, DT provides the same valid input to these implementations and observes differences in their executions to detect bugs. GDSmith [ 18] and Grand [ 72] are the earliest GDBMS testing techniques that are built on top of DT. MT detects bugs by first identifying relationships between multiple inputs and their corresponding outputs, and then checking whether the relationships are preserved for software executions.
mentions.context_after: These existing techniques target all different kinds of bugs that arise in all stages of the GDBMS workflow. Although offering the potential advantage of comprehensive bug detection, they may lose coverage for detecting a specific kind of bug. Various recent studies have shown that dedicated techniques for specific types of bugs are surprisingly effective, e.g., techniques for detecting task cancellation-related bugs [ 49], update bugs [ 71], performance bugs [ 23], configuration bugs [ 63], and Go data races [ 13]. mentions.sentence: For optimization bugs due to inaccurate cost estimations or defective plan space exploration algorithms, previous works on DBMS testing [ 11,21,45,46] also frequently report them.

While this again offers strong expressive power, it also introduces more complex scope semantics and execution models compared to SQL. Due to the significant differences in data storage formats and query languages for DBMSs and GDBMSs, the optimization bugs should have certain differences. Indeed, our findings 2 and 3 show that between one third and one half of the query optimization bugs for GDBMSs arise due to the complexities of graph representation and Cypher language.
mentions.context_after: Thus, the query optimization bugs in GDBMSs and DBMSs also share similarities.5 Bug Manifestation Study This section discusses the findings about how the optimization bugs can be manifested, and these findings can guide the design of testing techniques. mentions.sentence: However, most existing GDBMS testing techniques do not support the subquery clause kind at all, including GDSmith [ 18], GAMERA [ 75], GraspDB [ 32], GRev [ 36], Gslicer [35], and GQS [ 62]).
mentions.context_before: clause is used by 32% of bug-exposing queries. More specifically, among those queries that use the subquery clause kind, some of them use subquery clauses in a nested way. For instance, Figure 9agives the bug-exposing query for the issue Neo4j-12760 and the query uses the CALL{} subquery in a nested way. For subqueries, the optimizer must balance both the efficiency of graph pattern matching and subquery dependencies, thus it is no surprising that issues arise easily. In particular, note that Cypher employs explicit scope partitioning and variable flow control, further exacerbating the issue.

analysis.summary: A characteristic study of query optimization bugs in graph database systems, covering root causes, how the bugs manifest and how they are fixed, from which the authors draw ten findings. Building on the study they developed a testing tool aimed specifically at graph query optimization, which found 20 unique bugs, 10 of them optimization bugs.
analysis.narrative: The comparison here is against the graph-database descendants of SQLancer's techniques rather than SQLancer itself: GDsmith, GAMERA, GRev, GraspDB, GraphGenie and Gslicer are the seven state-of-the-art techniques the tool is measured against, several of them built on metamorphic testing and several co-authored by SQLancer's authors. SQLancer's own work is cited for the cost-estimation class of optimization bug and for the 24-hour evaluation methodology.
